papers.title: Multi-Structure Segmentation of Type B Aortic Dissection from CT Images with U-Net
papers.abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) is a life-threatening condition in which a tear in the intimal layer separates the aortic wall into a true and a false lumen. Assessment of the lumen, the intimal flap, and false-lumen thrombosis from CT images is important for risk analysis and treatment planning. This work applied U-Net-based deep neural networks to the automatic segmentation of these structures in TBAD. We collected 46 CT scans from 20 patients, with voxel-wise annotations of three structures: the aortic lumen, the intimal flap, and the thrombus. We explored four models: two convolutional networks, nnU-Net 2D and 3D, and two transformer-based architectures, TransUNet 2D and 3D. We observed that (1) for both nnU-Net and TransUNet, the 3D models outperformed their 2D counterparts on all three structures. The difference was small for the aortic lumen but large for the thin flap and the thrombus. The best model, nnU-Net 3D, reached a DSC of 93.05% for the lumen, 50.22% for the flap, and 69.94% for the thrombus. (2) The intimal flap was the most difficult structure for all models. Even the best 3D models showed large thrombus boundary errors in a few scans. These results provide a baseline for developing more advanced models for accurate segmentation of these structures in TBAD.

papers.title: Population-level emulation enables fast Bayesian calibration of cardiac digital twins
papers.abstract: Purpose: Patient-specific cardiac digital twins have the potential to guide individualized therapy, but generating these in a routine clinical workflow remains challenging. This is especially true when the twins must carry quantified uncertainty: Bayesian calibration requires thousands of simulations per patient, and the emulators that reduce this cost are typically trained one patient at a time. We aimed to train a single emulator across a patient cohort, so that a new patient can be calibrated in minutes without new simulations. Methods: We trained a population-level Gaussian process emulator whose inputs included a 12-dimensional latent encoding of the clinical features of each patient, so that a single emulator represents the whole cohort. We compared spending simulation budgets on resampling the real cohort with augmenting the cohort with digital chimeras, synthetic patients interpolated between real patients. Seven parameters of a closed-loop heart and circulation model were calibrated by Markov chain Monte Carlo to ten clinical biomarkers in 26 patients with left bundle branch block, each using an emulator trained without that patient, and the calibrated posteriors were compared against the full simulator. Results: A single emulator, trained without the held-out patient, calibrated the digital twin of each patient in 59.7-63.0 s per patient, versus 15 h with the simulator. Resampling the real cohort was the more efficient training strategy, bringing every output to R2 greater than or equal to 0.9, which augmentation did not achieve for the same simulation budget. For held-out patients, both strategies performed comparably (median leave-one-out normalized root-mean-square error 11.0% vs. 10.7%; p = 0.745), and error rose with distance from the cohort centroid (Spearman rho = +0.406). The calibrated models showed no cohort-wide bias (median standardized residual -0.12 against the clinical targets), and 95% predictive intervals contained 78.5% of targets, with the largest misfit in systolic blood pressure. Conclusion: Removing the need for new simulations for every new patient is a meaningful step toward uncertainty-aware cardiac digital twins that fit within a routine clinical workflow. Because the simulator, surrogate and sampler are interchangeable, the approach used here can be applied to other (cardiac) models and cohorts.

papers.title: Single-Component Photo-Crosslinked Lipoic Acid Functionalized Mucin Hydrogels: Dynamic Mucus Mimetics for Antiviral Protection
papers.abstract: Native mucus protects epithelial surfaces through viscoelastic networks of disulfide-linked mucins. However, commercially available mucins often fail to reconstitute comparable mechanical and barrier properties, while synthetic and hybrid mucus mimetics require polymeric crosslinkers that may alter mucus-like composition. Inspired by the native architecture, we directly functionalized porcine gastric and bovine submaxillary mucins with -lipoic acid to develop a single-component, photo-crosslinkable hydrogels. Upon UV irradiation (365 nm), the modified mucins rapidly form disulfide-crosslinked networks without added photo-initiator/ polymeric crosslinkers, two orders of magnitude faster as compared with PEG-SH approaches. The resulting mucin-lipoic acid (MUC-LA) hydrogels exhibit mucus-relevant properties, including tunable viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, self-healing, and size-dependent restrictions on nanoparticle transport. In transwell-based infection models, MUC-LA hydrogels (2-3%) mimicking the healthy airway mucus (G' {approx} 10-20 Pa) suppress epithelial infection by SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. Crosslinked MUC-LA provides greater protection against SARS-CoV-2 than the non-crosslinked, whereas both formulations suppress influenza A infection, suggesting distinct contributions from network formation and mucin-associated interactions. These findings establish a dynamic, mucus-mimetic platform integrating rapid photo-gelation, controllable mechanics, selective transport, and antiviral barrier functionality. MUC-LA hydrogels offer opportunities to investigate mucosal transport and host-pathogen interactions, with potential applications in drug delivery, and as biomaterials.

papers.title: A Fibrous Optofluidic Probe for Endovascular Sensing of Blood Oxygenation and Flow Velocity
papers.abstract: Local hemodynamic information including blood oxygenation and flow velocity could guide vascular interventions, yet obtaining these parameters in deep, narrow vessels remains challenging. Here, we report a flexible, submillimeter-scale fibrous optofluidic probe for endovascular sensing of blood oxygenation and flow velocity. The probe integrates a polymer optical fiber for light transmission with a microfluidic tube for dye injection, enabling spectroscopic oximetry and fluorescence dilution-based velocimetry through a single device. Via vascular intervention, we demonstrate local hemodynamic sensing in rabbit arteries and angiography-guided deployment in canine carotid arteries. The probe captures local changes in blood oxygenation and flow velocity during vascular occlusion and reperfusion, revealing hemodynamic disturbances that are not reflected in peripheral monitors. These results illustrate the complementary information provided by local oximetry and velocimetry and establish a compact optofluidic platform for quantitative hemodynamic monitoring during vascular interventions.

papers.title: Broad-spectrum in situ genetic reprogramming of native microbiomes
papers.abstract: Complex microbial communities are found throughout terrestrial, aquatic, and animal-associated ecosystems. Genetic modification of discrete microbial taxa within native communities represents a powerful tool to study and augment microbiome functions. Herein, we develop Synthetic Phage Assisted Reprogrammable and Targetable Addition (SPARTA) as a one-step strategy for packaging, delivering, and integrating large synthetic DNA into a broad range of native microbiomes. SPARTA leverages a broad-spectrum synthetic phage particle for in situ genome engineering within complex soil, freshwater, and mammalian fecal microbiomes, reprogramming 59 native species across 16 families. By modulating SPARTA components, we further demonstrated tunability of SPARTA towards targeted microbiome population. Additionally, we built a novel companion tool to quantitatively identify engineered taxa, named 16S crRNA-guided inference of bacterial engineering sequencing or ScRibe-seq. The SPARTA-ScRibe-seq pipeline delivered and validated functional synthetic gene clusters in diverse native microbiomes while preserving the original microbial community structure. Together, this novel genome engineering framework constitutes an end-to-end programmable platform for rational and customizable reprogramming of native microbiomes.

papers.title: Decoupled Surface Engineering Enables Cell-Interactive Edible Microcarriers across Food-Grade Polysaccharides
papers.abstract: Edible microcarriers for cultivated meat must support cell expansion while also contributing appropriately to the properties of the final food product. Food-grade polysaccharides exemplify this design challenge: despite their desirable food-related functions, they generally provide limited support for cell adhesion. This limitation calls for a strategy that introduces cell-interactive functionality without constraining bulk material selection. Here, we developed a decoupled surface-engineering strategy in which a poly-L-lysine/tannic acid (PLL/TA) interface is constructed on preformed polysaccharide microcarriers to enable cell-supportive functionality to emerge through interactions with the culture environment. On alginate microcarriers, PLL/TA modification markedly enhanced initial cell attachment, with 83% of modified microcarriers supporting attached cells compared with no detectable attachment on bare alginate. Cell-covered area subsequently reached 63.74% by Day 6, compared with 9.64% on PLL-coated microcarriers and negligible coverage on bare alginate. The PLL/TA interface promoted the recruitment of culture-medium proteins, including fibronectin, supporting an adaptive mechanism in which a cell-supportive interface develops through protein recruitment rather than predefined protein presentation. Importantly, the same surface modification enhanced early cell attachment when extended to pectin and carrageenan microcarriers and to Hanwoo bovine and Handon porcine muscle cells. On carrageenan microcarriers, the proportion of cell-bearing microcarriers increased from 30% to 100% for Hanwoo bovine cells and from 10% to 100% for Handon porcine cells following PLL/TA modification. These findings establish an adaptive and transferable surface-engineering strategy that enables cell-interactive functionality to be engineered separately from bulk material selection, expanding the design space for edible microcarriers in cultivated meat production.

papers.title: A shared wireless acquisition core for cortical and peripheral recordings in freely moving mice
papers.abstract: Experiments in freely moving mice often require simultaneous recording of cortical, muscle and movement signals, but adding channels and peripheral sensors increases headstage burden and acquisition complexity. We developed an eight-channel wireless headstage that records six cortical channels and two neck-electrode channels, together with synchronized acceleration. Reassigning electrodes enables cardiac recording with the same electronics. The 13*11*3 mm board forms part of an approximately 1.2-g head-mounted assembly, with the battery carried separately on the back. With inputs internally shorted, root-mean-square noise was 0.176V over 0.5-100 Hz. In four mice with chemically induced seizures, recordings resolved distributed cortical activity and animal-level spectral changes. Subject-dependent evaluation of the seizure detector yielded an overlap-based event F1 of 0.893 +/- 0.022. During pseudo-online replay, inference-software processing took 46.394 +/- 0.363 ms per update. In a separate cohort, recordings revealed distinct coherence patterns associated with movement and social behavior, highlighting potential as biomarkers of behavior-related neural activity. Together, these results demonstrate concurrent cortical, muscle, and movement recording through a common acquisition chain, with electrode reassignment extending the same hardware to cardiac recording.

papers.title: Multi-material delivery strategies to create deferoxamine-functionalized collagen scaffolds for craniofacial bone repair
papers.abstract: Craniomaxillofacial (CMF) bone injuries are common and can occur secondary to trauma, bone resection, and congenital abnormalities. While the current standard of care remains allograft or autograft, tissue engineering approaches offer the opportunity for alternative regenerative solutions. Biomaterial design has been central in this effort, with a primary consideration being the incorporation of motifs into biomaterials that accelerate osteogenic differentiation of progenitor cells and subsequent mineral synthesis. However, angiogenic potency, and subsequent angiogenic-osteogenic coupling, represent a critical challenge, as poor angiogenic activity can impair regenerative healing. Deferoxamine (DFO) can mimic cellular hypoxia via iron chelation and has been used as an angiogenic factor. However, its size (<1 kDa) severely limits its retention in the wound area. Here, we report a multi-material approach to improve angiogenic coupling in an osteogenic biomaterial. We report methods to retain DFO in mineralized collagen scaffold via its binding to a second polymer, gelatin, that can be incorporated into the scaffold to boost angiogenic potency while maintaining its osteo-regenerative properties. We employed carbodiimide chemistry to attach DFO to a gelatin backbone and retained 79.6% of the drug over a 7-day culture. Using a composite drug-delivery approach that combines freely soluble DFO with gelatin-bound DFO into the mineralized collagen scaffold, drove increased mesenchymal stem cell metabolic activity and enhanced expression of angiogenic genes in culture over 14 days. This work provides a novel approach to advance acellular regenerative biomaterials for osteogenic-angiogenic coupling processes.

papers.title: Generative design of de novo AAV vectors with unique serological profiles
papers.abstract: More than 5000 monogenic diseases are potentially curable by replacing a single defective gene with one that functions normally. Currently, the only clinically approved vector able to effectively deliver a therapeutic gene to a target tissue is Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs). However, despite decades of work, only a handful of gene replacement therapies have been approved, and many patients remain ineligible for even those. A major barrier to broad adoption of AAV therapies is pre-existing immunity to AAVs, mediated by neutralizing antibodies (nAbs). It is potentially possible to change exposed capsid surfaces in AAV capsids to avoid nAb recognition. However, traditional techniques such as rational design and directed evolution only allow modest changes. AAV function becomes compromised long before full nAb avoidance is achieved. Recent advances in protein design by generative modelling provide a new way to overcome this problem by learning AAV design constraints from natural sequences. We built a variational autoencoder that could learn these sequence constraints and generate functional AAV capsid proteins de novo. More than 255 designs were synthesized and tested in vitro in two design sets, with one set dedicated to exploring uncertain regions of the sequence space. Between the two campaigns, seven designs transduced human cells with >50% efficiency, of which four avoided nAb neutralization (NT50 < 1:50) in all human sera that were reactive to AAV. In one of these designs, sequence identity to the nearest natural AAV sequence was 18% divergent. Given the radical sequence diversity and its unique serological profile, this new capsid design would represent the first ever AAV serotype designed de novo.

papers.title: Agile manufacturing of PDMS microfluidic devices for cell culture without a clean room
papers.abstract: Microfluidic devices control fluid flow and the cellular microenvironment, and their fabrication usually relies on photolithography in a clean room. For devices with features of hundreds of micrometers to millimeters, this route is slow and costly, especially during prototyping, when the design changes after each test. Here, we describe and benchmark a workflow to fabricate polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) devices from laser-cut master molds, with equipment accessible to most biology laboratories. We cut three inexpensive materials, poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), polystyrene and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) tape, over a grid of laser power and speed and measured each cut by scanning electron microscopy. Cut depth and width increased line-arly with the laser energy delivered per unit length, which gives a simple rule to choose the settings for each material. We then bonded the PDMS replicas to glass without a plasma cleaner, by stopping curing early, once the replica could be demolded, and completing it in contact with the glass. Without any surface treatment, these devices held up to about 400 mbar; activating the glass with a handheld corona device raised this to about 900 mbar, enough for perfusion. The master material set the surface of the device: PMMA gave smooth replicas, whereas PVC tape gave rough walls. A three-channel device molded on PMMA held two cell-laden gels in place with phase guides and supported the co-culture of cancer cells and fibroblasts under perfusion. Further analysis of flow laminarity and different mixer designs confirmed the robustness of this method. This workflow takes a digital design to a working de-vice within a day and lets biology laboratories adapt microfluidic devices to their experiments without the need of a clean room.

papers.title: Tissue-like Viscoelasticity Drives Muscle Stem Cell Expansion Through Mechanical Memory Formation
papers.abstract: Mechanical cues are potent regulators of stem cell fate, with even transient exposure to substrates with varied elastic stiffness driving persistent changes in cell fate. Such elastic mechanical memory contributes to the loss of regenerative potential in skeletal muscle stem cells (MuSCs) when cultured on rigid substrates, hampering the translation of myogenic cell replacement therapies. Beyond elastic mechanical properties, cells also respond to time-dependent, viscoelastic mechanical properties, such as stress relaxation. However, whether tissue-like viscoelasticity can impart a mechanical memory that directs stem cell fate remains an open question. Accordingly, dual-network hydrogel biomaterials with decoupled control of stiffness, stress relaxation, and adhesive ligand presentation were engineered to recapitulate the viscoelastic mechanical properties of native muscle. Muscle-like viscoelastic substrates promote in vitro MuSC activation and accelerate stem cell expansion, matching in vivo activation timescales. Mechanistically, physiological viscoelasticity promotes focal adhesion stabilization and enhances Rac-Akt signaling, establishing a viscoelastic mechanical memory that supports progenitor expansion and persistent maintenance of a stem-like phenotype. These findings identify matrix viscoelasticity as a potent and persistent regulator of MuSC fate and provide a framework for engineering biomaterials that preserve MuSC stemness and expansion ex vivo.

papers.title: Receptor-guided engineering of oncolytic vaccinia creates a synthetic support niche for off-the-shelf NK cell therapy
papers.abstract: Combining adoptive cell therapy with oncolytic viruses offers a means to provide localized support within solid tumors, yet viral chassis and therapeutic payloads are often selected independently of the biological state of the manufactured cell product. Here, we establish an engineering framework that uses the phenotypic and functional features of an adoptive cell product as design inputs for a complementary oncolytic niche. Using off-the-shelf expanded, frozen, and thawed (EFT) natural killer (NK) cells as a model system, we identified manufacturing-associated reductions in chemokine responsiveness, dependence on extrinsic cytokine support, and loss of sustained function at limiting effector-to-target ratios. In a head-to-head evaluation under human NK-cell antiviral pressure, oncolytic vaccinia virus (VV) retained replication and spread, whereas HSV-1 was rapidly restricted, establishing VV as a compatible viral chassis. Mapping endogenous receptor expression and applying sequential functional screening under increasingly limiting effector densities then prioritized a five-factor program comprising CXCL11, IL-15, IL-27, IL-2, and IL-1{beta} that supported NK-cell migration, survival, cytotoxicity, and metabolic fitness at effector-to-target ratios as low as 1:10. Consolidating these signals into a single viral chassis increased antitumor activity but revealed a systemic inflammatory liability associated with constitutive IL-1{beta} expression. We therefore placed the IL-2/IL-1{beta} module under chemically inducible control, retaining in vivo antitumor activity while limiting systemic toxicity. Together, these findings establish a framework in which the post-manufacturing state of an adoptive cell product guides viral chassis selection, payload prioritization, and programmable control of a complementary oncolytic support niche.

papers.title: Synergy-informed bilevel optimization reveals joint-specific benefits for realistic exoskeleton torque prediction
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven optimization can guide exoskeleton control design, but its utility is limited by the accuracy with which muscle coordination is predicted. Strict effort-minimization formulations predict non-physiological muscle shutdown under high exoskeleton assistance, leading to peak assistive torques that exceed values reported in human-in-the-loop experiments. We evaluated the accuracy of synergy-informed simulations at predicting assistance across four single-joint exoskeleton configurations: ankle plantarflexion, knee extension, hip flexion, and hip abduction. We implemented a bilevel optimization to predict a parameterized assistive torque that minimizes metabolic cost, with assisted muscle dynamics estimated via either effort-minimization simulations (minimizing muscle effort only) or synergy-informed simulations (minimizing muscle effort constrained to a synergy structure). We used experimental data from five unimpaired adults walking at their preferred speed and compared results descriptively between the two formulations within each subject. Assistance based on effort-minimization simulations shut down agonist muscle activations and overestimated peak assistive torque compared with experimental values. In contrast, constraining muscle controls to a synergy structure prevented non-physiological muscle shutdown and yielded assistive torques closer to those measured in human-in-the-loop experiments. This benefit was not observed equally across all assisted degrees of freedom or subjects, emerging only where no single synergy could be suppressed to unload the assisted muscles. Synergy weights can therefore be interpreted as joint-specific predictors of when simulations can reliably inform wearable robot design.

papers.title: A Continuum Fibre Network Model for the Anisotropic and Compressible Mechanics of Human Skin
papers.abstract: We present a Continuum Fibre Network (CFN) formulation for modelling anisotropy, strain stiffening and volume change in fibrous soft tissues. The model combines a three-dimensional fibre orientation distribution, a bilinear tensile fibre law and a separate phenomenological volumetric potential. We calibrated the model using published uniaxial tensile and volume-change data for excised human skin from separate studies. Changes in cross-sectional area affected the tensile stress estimates for models that predicted volume change. Simulations of indentation, shear and biaxial tension illustrate predictions of the calibrated formulation under additional loading conditions. The CFN formulation included a weak isotropic neo-Hookean ground matrix with a prescribed shear modulus of 0.1 MPa.

papers.title: Citrate-Based Hydrogels Promote Closure of Infected Diabetic Wounds
papers.abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a significant threat to the quality of life for individuals with diabetes, affecting approximately 1.6 million patients in the US, as of 2023. When these wounds do not heal and become chronic wounds, they can become infected and increase the risk of digit and/or lower limb amputation. Therefore, there is a critical need for therapies that promote wound closure in the presence and absence of infection. We have previously reported the potential benefits of the thermoresponsive citrate-based macromolecule poly(polyethylene glycol citrate-co-N-isopropylacrylamide) (PPCN) in diabetic rodent and swine models of non-infected full thickness dermal wounds. In this study, we compared four PPCN formulations (PPCN, PPCN-CMOF, A5G81-PPCN, and A5G81-PPCN-CMOF), which are functionalized with the laminin-derived cell adhesion peptide A5G81 and/or contain entrapped copper metal-organic framework nanoparticles (CMOF) designed to release Cu2+ slowly, in diabetic mice with wounds infected with S. aureus. In infected wounds, all four formulations significantly improved cumulative closure relative to saline (adjusted p = 0.002-0.021). In non-infected wounds, only PPCN-CMOF significantly improved cumulative closure relative to saline (p = 0.046), although all four formulations reached [≥]95% closure earlier than saline (adjusted p = 0.009-0.045). In vitro, the CMOF-containing formulations produced the highest bacterial killing (90% for A5G81-PPCN-CMOF and 84% for PPCN-CMOF), whereas A5G81-PPCN and PPCN reduced bacterial colonies by 76% and 59%. PPCN modification with A5G81 and/or CMOF increased endothelial mesh formation in vitro. In vivo, PPCN-based formulations increased granulation tissue thickness and, depending on formulation and infection status, vascular marker expression. These results suggest that PPCN and PPCN formulations containing CMOF and/or A5G81 are a potentially viable technology that can be added to the wound care toolbox to accelerate healing of diabetic foot ulcers in the presence of infection. These findings support further investigation of PPCN as an instructive pro-regenerative biomaterial in a preclinical large animal model.

papers.title: An Accessible and Scalable Pipette-Driven Microfluidic Platform for Lipid Nanoparticle Formulation
papers.abstract: Advances in lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology have increased the need for accessible and scalable methods that accelerate low-volume formulation screening. Here, we describe a disposable microfluidic mixer actuated by a positive-displacement pipette equipped with dual-chamber pipette tip, providing volumetric control at a fixed flow rate ratio without external microfluidic pumps. Computational fluid dynamics analysis predicted shorter micromixing times in the high-shear spiral channel than in the low-shear design. Across three benchmark lipid formulations, the high-shear mixer reproducibly generated smaller LNPs with higher mRNA encapsulation efficiency than the low-shear mixer or manual pipetting. Orthogonal characterization further revealed higher particle concentrations, structural features consistent with compact particles, more uniform mRNA loading, and a lower empty-particle fraction. LNPs prepared using the selected high-shear mixer mediated functional mRNA delivery in 2D cell cultures, a 3D human liver tissue model, and mice. Integration with a liquid-handling robot enabled automated screening of formulation parameters. Dimensionless mixing-time analysis guided enlargement of the mixer geometry for a separate production system, which produced 75 mL preparations at 150 mL/min with particle size and mRNA encapsulation efficiency comparable to those obtained with the small-scale mixer. This platform provides an accessible, automation-compatible approach to LNP formulation screening and a route to larger-scale production.

papers.title: Mitochondrial transplantation redirects rather than suppresses the inflammatory response in primary human monocytes
papers.abstract: Circulating monocytes are recruited into inflamed tissue, where local cues determine whether the macrophages they become drive inflammation or resolve it. Because that decision occurs after cells leave the blood, the circulating stage offers a window to alter monocyte programming, and monocyte inflammatory function is closely coupled to mitochondrial metabolism. Here we transplanted freshly isolated, respiration-competent mitochondria from HEK293T cells into primary human CD14 monocytes and characterized the resulting mitochondria-transplanted monocytes (MTM) across surface phenotype, respiration, and inflammatory function. Isolated mitochondria were intact and respiration-competent, with a respiratory control ratio of 8.7 and a coupling efficiency of 78.9 %. Monocytes internalized them in proportion to the dose supplied; within 3 h, 88% of viable cells were positive for labeled mitochondria, with no loss of viability detected; isolated mitochondria did not activate NF-{kappa}B or IRF reporters in THP1-Dual cells. Transplantation reduced the frequency of the pro-inflammatory intermediate subset, increased CD14 by 2.11-fold and HLA-DR by 1.31-fold, and decreased CD163. MTM showed reduced ATP-linked respiration with maximal capacity preserved, and a trend toward a higher maximal-to-basal respiration ratio. Following stimulation with LPS, MTM released markedly less TNF- (0.06-fold) and CXCL10/IP-10 (0.25-fold) and, in most donors, more IL-10 (3.33-fold), while the remaining analytes were largely unchanged. Mitochondrial transplantation therefore shifts primary human monocytes toward a phenotype with selectively reduced inflammatory mediator release and increased IL-10 in most donors. It identifies circulating monocytes as a tractable target for mitochondria-based modulation of inflammation.

papers.title: Multimodal imaging links molecular identity with nanoscale-resolved 3D cell morphology in opossum cortical cultures
papers.abstract: In the mammalian central nervous system (CNS), the ability to regenerate after injury drops sharply in the first weeks after birth, but how this change is reflected in cell morphology and organization is still not fully understood. Here we cultivated cortical cell cultures from the gray short-tailed opossum (Monodelphis domestica) and compared cells derived from early postnatal pups (postnatal day 3-6, "Pyoung") with those from older pups (postnatal day 16-18, "Pold"), which differ in their capacity to regenerate after injury. For each culture, we assessed marker-defined cellular composition using fluorescently labeled markers for neurons, glia, and immature/progenitor cells, and characterized their nanoscale-resolved three-dimensional morphology using label-free scanning ion conductance microscopy (SICM). Pyoung cultures exhibited active change in shape over time, contained a higher proportion of immature SOX2 cells, and grew more neurites (TUJ1) into the lesion site after injury. Moreover, Pold cultures showed more stable soma size (e.g., thickness, area, volume), a larger astroglial (SOX9) population early in culture, and a glia-dominated lesion response. These early astroglia included more immature or reactive (vimentin) astrocytes. SICM further revealed cellular bridges across the lesion, ridges left in the substrate by the injury, and aligned neurite outgrowth. Across all measurements, changes in molecular markers were associated with corresponding changes in cell morphology. This multimodal combination of fluorescence labeling and SICM therefore relates marker-defined cellular composition to physical organization across micro- and nanoscale features during and after postnatal in vitro development.

papers.title: Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.

papers.title: Distinct mechanical signatures of dairy and plant-based cheeses
papers.abstract: Plant-based cheeses account for about 1% of U.S. retail cheese sales and often fail to match the texture and flavor of dairy cheese. Here we compare three commercial dairy and plant-based pairs, cheddar, feta, and mozzarella, with texture profile analysis (n = 60), tension, compression, and shear tests (n = 219), constitutive artificial neural networks, and a consumer panel (n = 306). Plant mozzarella is at least five times stiffer than dairy mozzarella at small strain, yet softer and less cohesive under 50% compression. Plant feta matches the initial stiffness of dairy feta but shows a peak in its shear response. Plant cheddar differs in both stiffness and shear response. Model discovery selects first-invariant models for all six cheeses, but no model term separates the two groups. Consumers rate 68--78% of attributes "just about right" for dairy cheeses and 29--38% for plant-based cheeses. These single-product comparisons define product-specific targets for plant-based cheese design.

papers.title: PROST: An Open Toolbox, Harmonised Multi-Lab Dataset, and Meta-Analysis of Ankle-Foot Roll-Over Shape
papers.abstract: The ankle-foot roll-over shape (ROS) is the sagittal-plane path of the centre of pressure (CoP) during the stance phase of walking, expressed in a shank-based coordinate system. It describes the effective rocker geometry that emerges from both the shape and the elastic deformation of the ankle-foot system during walking, and informs prosthetic and orthotic design. Previous studies characterised ROS in small samples with differing laboratory protocols, so they have not systematically assessed inter-individual variability or its relation to anthropometrics. We developed the open-source Public ROS Toolbox (PROST) for standardised ROS computation, and used it to harmonise marker trajectories, ground reaction forces and CoP data from four public gait datasets collected in independent laboratories. For each leg, we fitted a circular arc to the pooled ROS of all its stance phases. In a one-stage individual-participant data meta-analysis, linear mixed-effects models, with dataset as a fixed effect and participant as a random intercept, related the arc radius and the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre to anthropometrics, and, in the two self-selected-speed datasets, to walking speed. The harmonised dataset comprises 249 participants and 5,667 stance phases at walking speeds of 0.7-8.5 km/h. Circular arcs fitted the ROS closely (mean RMS radial residual 1.9 mm). The radius had a median of 410.3 mm (interquartile range, IQR, 237.6 mm), and the circle centre lay posterior to the ankle (median -20.6 mm, IQR 49.5 mm). Between-participant differences, quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), accounted for 42% of the variance in log radius (95% CI 25-57%) and 47% of the variance in the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre (95% CI 24-65%). Anthropometrics explained a negligible share of this variance (radius: pseudo-R2 -0.001, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.12), and height normalisation did not reduce radius variability (robust coefficient of variation 43% with and without normalisation). Faster self-selected walking was associated with a larger radius and a more posterior circle centre. To our knowledge, this study provides the first harmonised multi-lab ROS dataset. Together with the open-source toolbox, it is publicly available to support reproducible research in gait biomechanics, rehabilitation device design and clinical gait assessment. ROS geometry was participant-specific but was not predicted by age, sex, height or mass. A device ROS scaled from anthropometrics is therefore unlikely to match an individual's ROS, motivating studies of whether matching it, through device geometry and stiffness, improves gait mechanics.

papers.title: Engineered microvessel networks -- Longitudinal transcriptomic profiling validates chip-grown tissues as a robust model for studying vasculature
papers.abstract: Vascularised Organ-on-Chip (OoC) models are promising New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), but their translation requires validation for defined Contexts of Use (CoU). Here, we combine microfluidic microvessel networks (MVNs) with longitudinal bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing to determine how cell provenance influences engineered vascular phenotype. Stromal cell identity produced distinct network architectures and transcriptional trajectories, demonstrating that support cells, commonly treated as interchangeable, represent an important CoU variable. Primary human pancreatic microvascular endothelial cells failed to form stable perfusable networks, but supplementation with 10% Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) or Blood Outgrowth Endothelial Cells (BOECs) rescued self-assembly. Single-cell transcriptomics identified specialised endothelial populations associated with vascular morphogenesis, including tip, stalk, phalanx, endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) and pericyte-like endothelial cells. Failed networks lacked coherent endothelial specialisation, whereas rescued networks restored stabilising cell states and revealed FLRT2--UNC5B signalling within pericyte-like HUVECs, recapitulating a pathway implicated in angiogenic development in vivo. These findings establish cell provenance as a critical determinant of microvascular NAM performance and demonstrate how transcriptomic validation can define and strengthen the biological relevance of microvessel-on-chip models for specific CoUs.

papers.title: From Fill to Freeze: Redesigning homeRNA to Enable Robust Sampling and Scalable Downstream Processing Workflows for Remote Blood Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: In-person research can introduce barriers to participation, including proximity to a study site and scheduling constraints. Our lab developed the homeRNA platform to address these barriers, enabling remote blood collection and RNA stabilization for transcriptomic research. To increase the applicability of homeRNA for large-scale studies, a redesigned version was developed with modifications to 1) improve usability for both participants and downstream processing laboratories, 2) allow for high-throughput manufacturing, and 3) extend the shelf life of the stabilizer tube. In this work, we systematically tested this design against anticipated stresses that can occur throughout a remote study (e.g., high temperature exposure during shipment) to identify and characterize its limitations. We found that the homeRNA device can be prepared and stored at room temperature at least three months in advance of sampling with continued shelf life analysis underway. We also found that the homeRNA platform produces RNA of sufficient quality for downstream transcriptomic analysis under standard shipping durations (i.e., 2 days in transit) and ambient-to-high temperature conditions (i.e., 25-40 {degrees}C) and that RNA quality is unaffected by variable blood volumes collected by participants (mean RIN=7.8 in blood volumes 0.25-1 mL). Lastly, we also found that samples can be stored in typical cold storage temperatures and even up to standard room temperature for at least 4 weeks (mean RIN=8.1 after 4 weeks of storage at -80 to 20 {degrees}C). This work validates that the new homeRNA platform is robust to many of the expected stresses that samples can experience during remote studies.

papers.title: Commensal Engineered Living Materials for Sustained Secretome Delivery and Wound Healing
papers.abstract: Using living cells as dynamic biological factories offers immense potential for the continuous, localized production of therapeutic proteins within compromised tissues. This strategy is particularly compelling for treating chronic non-healing wounds, which lack therapeutics that are able to function effectively in the inflammatory microenvironment. Commensal bacteria have been shown to promote healing in these hostile microenvironments, yet applying live microbes directly onto compromised tissue is clinically unfeasible due off-target safety risks and engraftment challenges. Herein, we establish a well-defined commensal Engineered Living Material (cELM) that allows encapsulation, retention, function, and delivery of native beneficial bacteria for localized production and release of a pro-healing secretome over weeks. We specifically encapsulated a pro-healing human wound bacterial isolate, Alcaligenes faecalis, using biocompatible, click-reactive hydrogel building blocks (thiol- or vinyl-sulfone-functionalized multi-arm poly(ethylene glycol)) and systematically varied the density of the polymer network and of the encapsulated bacteria to establish design rules for creating pro-healing cELMs. Physical confinement in the hydrogel network ensured bacterial biocontainment, while the hydrogel mesh size still permitted diffusion of the therapeutic secretome. Notably, controlling encapsulation density revealed an inverse relationship wherein lower cell densities yielded significantly enhanced per-cell metabolic activity and provided sustained production of pro-healing secreted factors. In a murine diabetic wound model, these A. faecalis cELMs shielded the encapsulated bacteria from host clearance, maintained biocontainment, accelerated re-epithelialization, and improved wound bed maturity. Together, these findings establish design principles for cELMs that couple bacterial biocontainment with sustained secretome delivery, providing a promising platform for localized treatment of chronic wounds.

papers.title: Preserving Nanotherapy-Induced Allogeneic Murine Islet Graft Tolerance During Distal Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infection
papers.abstract: Eliminating lifelong immunosuppression can make islet transplantation a durable alternative to insulin therapy for type 1 diabetes. As short-course tolerogenic regimens are developed to replace lifelong immunosuppression, it is critical to test their robustness against perturbations such as hospital-acquired infections, which transplant recipients routinely encounter. Herein, we investigated whether rapamycin-loaded polymersomes (rPS), a subcutaneous nanotherapy that induces long-term murine islet allograft survival, can preserve host defenses in a Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) skin infection, and whether the resulting immune response from this distal infection relative to graft location erodes rPS-induced tolerance. rPS maintained neutrophil antibacterial activity despite inhibiting oxidative mechanisms in vitro, and rPS-treated mice demonstrated normal recovery following MRSA challenge. However, MRSA skin infection caused a decline of ~43% in recipient survival for rPS-treated mice, despite surviving recipients retaining glucose-stimulated insulin responsiveness. This erosion of allograft acceptance coincided with a burst of IL-6 within 24h of the infection followed by elevated TNF-[a] and neutrophilia at 13 days post-infection. Combining rPS with a single dose of methylprednisolone reduced IL-6 and TNF- without altering neutrophilia, nearly doubling survival among infected recipients to 80%. Our findings demonstrate that partial dampening of inflammatory insults can restore superior islet allograft acceptance following perioperative infection.

papers.title: Extensional Flow Microfluidics Reveal Size-Dependent Core-Shell Mechanical Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Tumor Spheroids
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanical behavior of cancer cell aggregates is important for investigating metastatic potential and developing effective therapeutics. Tumor cell clusters are major contributors to metastasis and can undergo extreme deformation to migrate through capillaries smaller than the cluster size, suggesting complex multicellular mechanics. Despite their clinical significance, the mechanics of multicellular spheroids remain underexplored. In this study, the mechanical behavior of spheroids formed from the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 was investigated using a cross-slot microfluidic device. Suspended spheroids from two size ranges were stretched in non-contact extensional flow (small spheroids mostly 40 < D0 < 75 m, large spheroids mostly 90 < D0 < 145 m). Digital image correlation analyses of intra-spheroid strains revealed strong deformation differences for small and large spheroids while analyses based on 2D projected contours of the spheroid shape did not show trends. Smaller spheroids deformed relatively homogeneously and exhibited significant overall stretching. In contrast, larger spheroids displayed heterogeneous deformation characterized by a stiff central core and a deformable outer shell. To investigate the origin of these mechanical differences, cellular morphology and the expression of stiffness-associated proteins, including vimentin and E-cadherin, were assessed from confocal microscopy. Larger spheroids display significantly lower nuclear sphericity than small spheroids, indicating more cellular packing with increasing spheroid size. Additionally, vimentin expression was concentrated in the outer shell of large spheroids, whereas small spheroids exhibit vimentin expression throughout the aggregate. Thus individual cell morphology and cytoskeletal networks seemed to contribute to the core-shell biomechanical behavior of the large spheroids and lack thereof for small spheroids. Taken together, this study suggests that as spheroids grow, they transition from an irregular and disorganized cluster at low cell numbers to a coordinated and hierarchical structure at sufficient cell numbers that corresponds to diameters {gtrsim} 100 m.

papers.title: MitoDecode: quantitative phenotypic decoding of mitochondrial stress states from fluorescence images
papers.abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images. MitoDecode eliminates the need for mitochondrial segmentation, is parameter-free, and operates across both diffraction-limited and super-resolution optical imaging modalities. It assigns a phenotypic probability profile for each individual cell, indicating both type and severity of phenotypic stress. The readout thus enables comparisons between different stressors and provides clues for underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, the method captures phenotypic shifts continuously across treatment doses, revealing subtle variations that would otherwise be missed. We demonstrate MitoDecode's adaptability across diverse cell types, imaging modalities, and stress conditions, and show that it can reliably detect mitochondrial phenotypes, even when stressors target non-mitochondrial pathways. We validate the reliability of the model with biochemical assays, showcase its utility for phenotypic stress profiling of drug treatments, and envisage its application for early-stage disease detection, drug discovery, and mechanistic lead generation.

papers.title: Material context and TGF-β blockade timing determine retained matrix in patient-derived bioprinted keratoconus stroma
papers.abstract: Stromal repair requires newly formed matrix to persist while the contractile response to TGF-{beta} is controlled. We developed patient-derived bioprinted gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) stroma to connect material-dependent cell responses with matrix retention after timed receptor blockade. In constructs from six keratoconus (KC) and six normal donors, KC cells retained disease-associated transcription while secreting procollagen I and lumican at normal-donor levels per unit DNA. Comparisons with two-dimensional culture and matched cast GelMA showed that the three-dimensional environment increased matrix induction and lowered resting contractile expression. Printing added a stromal identity response that persisted as retained lumican. Delayed blockade after a TGF-{beta}1 pulse preserved matrix transcription and late secretion. Eleven days after withdrawal, this finite course left more native collagen and lower contractile-gene expression than vehicle in 9/12 donors. Across the tested blockade regimens, at least one regimen achieved both outcomes at the final endpoint in 11/12 donors, including every KC donor. Culture format changed the preferred regimen. Choosing finite blockade by retained collagen instead of secretion changed the schedule in half the donors; the selected arms contained 22.2% more collagen. Retained collagen and contractile expression therefore provide joint endpoints for designing when TGF-{beta}-pathway courses, including losartan and TGF-{beta}3 treatment for keratoconic and scarred corneas, should start and stop.

papers.title: Unlocking Targeted Underwater Delivery of Coral Probiotics
papers.abstract: The rapid global decline of coral reefs has intensified the need for innovative conservation strategies, including microbial therapies to enhance coral health and resilience. A major limitation, however, is the lack of effective delivery systems for administering Beneficial Microorganisms for Corals (BMCs). In this study, we present natural, biodegradable systems for the underwater delivery of probiotic bacteria to corals. Three customized alginate-based delivery formats (beads, hydrogels, and filaments) were developed and loaded with the probiotic Pseudoalteromonas peptidolytica. The materials were loaded with the bacterium at an average concentration of 10^(4) CFU/g of dry polymer and engineered to sink underwater while keeping their structural integrity over time. In vitro assays showed controlled release kinetics, with encapsulated probiotics remaining viable and capable of replication. In vivo experiments compared syringe-based inoculation with the application of alginate beads, hydrogels, and filaments to corals. Microbiome analyses performed before and after inoculation confirmed successful probiotic colonization following deployment of the alginate-based delivery systems. Relative abundance of the probiotic genus Pseudoalteromonas increased markedly in treated corals, reaching 11.5 % after 48 h with alginate beads, 12.7 % after 48 h with hydrogels, and 12.6 % after 24 h with filaments. Furthermore, the degradation mechanisms of the three delivery systems were investigated. As the first biomaterial-based underwater delivery systems specifically engineered for coral probiotics, these alginate-based materials provide a promising foundation for advancing microbial therapies in both controlled aquaria and natural reef environments.

papers.title: 1D model simulations suggest biofilms can suppress cathodic H2 bubble formation
papers.abstract: Microbial electrosynthesis (MES) electrochemically generates H2 for the reduction of CO2 into acetate by acetogens. So far, the importance of a biofilm on the cathode of such systems remains under debate. Here, we investigated the role of cathodic biofilms through computational modelling. We developed MES-BIOFILM, a comprehensive one-dimensional model to simulate steady-state H2 and CO2 concentration gradients within cathodic biofilms, while accounting for the limited solubility of H2. The effects of key biofilm properties, including thickness, cell density and H2 consumption rate were analysed. Overall, our simulations indicate that cathodic biofilms play an important role in (1) minimizing H2 loss from the system through H2 consumption within the biofilm; and (2) suppressing H2 bubble formation by maintaining the H2 concentrations at the cathode surface below saturation. Our model predicts that the current density at which H2 bubbles begin to form can be increased by 5.5-fold relative to a bare electrode when biofilms exhibit a high cell density and high H2 consumption rate. This effect requires biofilms of at least 50 m thickness, whereas CO2 diffusion limitations arise above 200 m. These findings highlight the critical role of biofilms to increase MES performance, while requiring further experimental validation.
